Priming-induced transcription returned to baseline by day 12 while protection was still shown at challenge (timing not in the abstract), so the protective state is not carried by sustained transcription; decay of protection itself not tested. Stage (likely spat as in de Kantzow) not stated in the abstract, so left as not reported. Full text is CC BY but was not retrievable here (ScienceDirect blocked; not in PMC; scite had no text)

stressor: sublethal live Vibrio europaeus (CECT 8136), oral exposure by immersion
dose_treatment: live V. europaeus at ~10^6 CFU/mL in filtered seawater (immersion, uptake by filtration) vs 0.22-um filtered seawater only; 8-month-old juveniles 13 mm shell length; ~19 C
duration: 7 d (168 h post-priming) in 100 mL bath with aeration; food and water renewal at day 5 (120 hpp)
challenge: lethal oral V. europaeus challenge at ~10^7 CFU/mL by 24 h immersion then 8 h emersion, 168 hpp; mortality recorded to 80 hpi (to 164 hpi in primed clams)
persistence_days: ~2 (bath water renewed at 120 hpp; challenge at 168 hpp, i.e. 7 d after priming began; clams still carried ~10^2 V. europaeus copies/mg at challenge)
readouts: survival (Kaplan-Meier, log-rank); V. europaeus load by TaqMan qPCR (genome copies/mg tissue) through priming and challenge; microbiota by full-length 16S rRNA (PacBio) through priming and challenge
effect_magnitude: 87% survival in primed-challenged clams vs 0% in non-primed (100% mortality within 56 hpi), p<0.0001 (log-rank; figure legend says p<0.001); primed-challenged vs primed-unchallenged p=0.0117; no mortality during priming; pathogen fell from 3.21x10^4 to 4.15x10^2 copies/mg in first 48 hpp; after challenge primed clams peaked at 5.07x10^5 copies/mg (32 hpi) then fell to 3.37x10^3 (56 hpi) and 1.54x10^2 (164 hpi), whereas non-primed never fell below ~10^5
replication: 6 tanks per condition (3 for survival, 3 for DNA sampling), 15 juveniles per tank; 3 conditions (non-primed challenged, primed challenged, primed unchallenged); microbiota from one pooled sample of 3 clams per time point (no biological replication)
notes: First oral (immersion) priming in Manila clam, using live pathogen at a natural infection route; compare injection-based Li_2025a in the same species (authors cite 82% survival and 69% priming-phase survival there vs 87% and no priming mortality here). Pathogen persisted at low non-lethal levels (~10^2 copies/mg) in primed clams throughout - a carrier risk for applied use. A priming-associated microbiota (Acinetobacter, Brevundimonas, Sphingobium, Psychrobacter) established by 144 hpp and re-emerged after challenge; Arcobacteraceae rose with mortality in non-primed clams. No host immune or gene expression assay (qPCR and 16S are pathogen/microbiota layers, hence molecular_layers None). No non-primed unchallenged group. Text reports peak at 32 hpi while Fig. 3 legend says 24 hpi

stressor: prior Vibrio parahaemolyticus exposure (immune training)
dose_treatment: not reported (prior V. parahaemolyticus exposure vs unexposed controls; live or inactivated, dose and route not stated in the abstract)
duration: not reported
challenge: secondary Vibrio parahaemolyticus challenge
readouts: early cumulative mortality after secondary challenge; DSCAM expression
effect_magnitude: Prior bacterial exposure associated with reduced early cumulative mortality upon secondary challenge and altered DSCAM expression (no numbers in the abstract)
notes: Only the immune-training experiment is extracted; the paper is mainly a hemocyte single-cell (10x scRNA-seq) atlas after primary infection, which identified infection-induced DSCAM alternative splicing in unresolved hemocytes. Assay used for DSCAM in the training arm is not stated in the abstract (Targeted qPCR is an assumption to be checked against full text). Effect described as early mortality only, so durability of protection through the full challenge is unclear. Full text paywalled; stage, dose and interval unknown; molecular_layers set to not reported: the abstract does not name the assay

stressor: formalin-killed Vibrio parahaemolyticus
dose_treatment: not reported (formalin-killed V. parahaemolyticus vs unprimed controls; dose and route not stated in the abstract)
duration: not reported
challenge: lethal challenge with live Vibrio parahaemolyticus
readouts: cumulative survival; hemolymph and serum antibacterial activity; antimicrobial peptide mRNA; TLR2-MyD88-Pelle-Dorsal pathway expression; melanin level and phenoloxidase activity; reactive oxygen production; catalase and peroxidase activity
effect_magnitude: Primed crabs had significantly improved cumulative survival after lethal live challenge, with earlier and higher hemolymph/serum antibacterial activity, upregulated AMP and TLR2-MyD88-Pelle-Dorsal genes, faster and stronger melanization (melanin, PO) and higher ROS, CAT and POD (abstract gives no numbers)
notes: Abstract obtained via the OpenAlex index; the gold-OA full text could not be retrieved (ScienceDirect blocked, not in PMC, no scite text). Same species and design family as Zhang_2020 (heat-killed V. parahaemolyticus, 7 d), here with formalin inactivation; the title stresses EARLY resistance, implying a humoral-led, possibly short-lived effect. Gene assay not named in the abstract (Targeted qPCR to be checked). Online 2025-12-24; issue year 2026; molecular_layers set to not reported: the abstract does not name the assay

stressor: oral formalin-killed AHPND Vibrio parahaemolyticus (bacterin vaccine), alone or after 7 d dietary Imuno-FS Plus (banana-stem powder) with a 0, 2, 4 or 6 d interval
dose_treatment: formalin-killed V. parahaemolyticus coated on feed at 10^8 CFU/g feed (10^8 CFU per shrimp) vs unvaccinated commercial diet (positive control); Imuno-FS Plus 0.75 g/kg feed in adjuvant arms; shrimp 4.06 g; 28-30 C, 20-22 ppt
duration: vaccine fed 4 consecutive days (4 feedings/d); Imuno-FS Plus 7 consecutive days before vaccination with 0 (simultaneous), 2, 4 or 6 d interval
challenge: AHPND V. parahaemolyticus challenge at 10^6 CFU/mL (LD50-based); mortality recorded 7 d
persistence_days: ~3 (pre-challenge sample D3AV taken 3 d after completion of vaccination; challenge followed)
readouts: survival and relative percent survival; hepatopancreas V. parahaemolyticus load (CFU/g) at 1, 3, 5, 7 d post-challenge; total hemocyte count; phagocytic activity; phenoloxidase; respiratory burst; hepatopancreas histopathology at day 3; qPCR of DSCAM, ProPO, LvBigPEN, peroxinectin, FREP
effect_magnitude: Survival: positive control 40.00+-9.13%, vaccine only 66.25+-11.09% (significantly above control by Tukey letters), adjuvant only 67.50+-8.66%, simultaneous AV 51.25+-13.15% (not different from control), A2V 73.75+-8.54%, A4V 83.75+-14.93%, A6V 80.00+-7.07%, unchallenged 92.50+-6.46%; RPS vaccine only 43.75%, A4V 72.92%, A6V 66.67%; hepatopancreas V. parahaemolyticus undetectable at day 7 in A4V and A6V vs 2.579 log CFU/g in positive control
replication: one 150-shrimp rearing tank per treatment during priming/vaccination (8 treatments), then 4 aquaria x 20 shrimp per treatment for challenge; 3 shrimp per treatment per sampling point for immune, gene and histology assays
notes: Included on the vaccine-only (V) arm: an oral inactivated-pathogen exposure with significant protection 3 d later. The Imuno-FS Plus component is a continuous dietary plant-extract immunostimulant, which by atlas precedent (Pandanus and leaf-extract exclusions) would not qualify on its own; the adjuvant-only arm protected as much as the vaccine alone. The paper's question is adjuvant-to-vaccine timing: simultaneous delivery gave no protection, interpreted as immune overstimulation. Pseudoreplication: each treatment schedule applied in a single tank before splitting into aquaria. V vs control significance read from Table 2 letters, not stated in text. No PMID; PMCID PMC13629208

species: Haliotis rubra; Haliotis laevigata; H. rubra x H. laevigata hybrid
stressor: poly(I:C) (synthetic dsRNA viral mimic) given to female broodstock
dose_treatment: not reported (poly(I:C) priming of female broodstock vs unprimed mothers; dose and route not stated in the abstract)
duration: priming 8 weeks, 4 weeks or 3 days before spawning (number of doses not stated)
challenge: HaHV-1 challenge of offspring at 12 months of age
persistence_days: ~368; ~393; ~421 (priming 3 d, 4 wk or 8 wk before spawning plus offspring challenged at 12 months)
readouts: offspring survival to HaHV-1 at 12 months; offspring weight and shell length at 6-12 months; broodstock spawning success
effect_magnitude: Maternal poly(I:C) at 8 wk, 4 wk or 3 d before spawning did not protect progeny against HaHV-1 at 12 months; offspring of primed mothers significantly smaller in weight and length than offspring of unprimed mothers; broodstock handling did not impair spawning (no numbers in the abstract)
notes: Negative TGIP result with a cost: no protection and smaller offspring (maladaptive trade-off). Authors highlight inherent HaHV-1 resistance of abalone under 1 year old, so the 12-month challenge may have been uninformative rather than TGIP being absent. Very long interval between maternal priming and offspring challenge relative to other TGIP studies. Three genetic groups combined in one row because the abstract does not report them as separate experiments. Within-generation poly(I:C) protection in abalone is prior work cited by the authors. Abstract obtained via the OpenAlex index; CC BY full text not retrievable here

stressor: diel-cycling hypoxia
dose_treatment: 0.5 mg/L dissolved oxygen (8% saturation) at trough vs 100% saturation normoxic control
duration: Phase 1: 18 d containing 13 d of diel cycling (3 h drawdown, 4 h plateau at 0.5 mg/L, 3 h ramp up, 14 h control), 5 d/week; Phase 2: 18 d containing 14 d cycling
challenge: second 18 d diel-cycling hypoxia exposure applied 60 d after the first (fully crossed CC/CH/HC/HH design)
readouts: gene-body DNA methylation; differentially methylated gene counts (companion paper measured tissue and shell growth)
effect_magnitude: 196 DMGs between CH and HC; only 12 DMGs CC vs HC; 1 DMG (MDE1) CC vs HH; 0 DMGs HH vs CH; first exposure PERMANOVA R2=0.068 p=0.017 and second R2=0.076 p=0.004 across all genes; DMG-only ordination explained ~60% of variation; 0.25-1.00% of CpGs methylated
concordance: Discordant (methylome differences driven mainly by the FIRST exposure whereas the companion phenotype paper found growth driven mainly by the SECOND exposure)
replication: 12 tanks (6 per treatment) in Phase 1 with 150 oysters per container; 48 oysters per tank in Phase 2; n=5 individuals per treatment combination for methylRAD
notes: Molecular carryover effect explicitly decoupled from gross phenotype. Recent exposure overrode earlier exposure (HH vs CH = 0 DMGs). Whole-body tissue may mask tissue-specific signal; methylRAD gives low coverage; no paired gene expression. Uses the ambient-temperature subset of the Donelan et al. 2021 animals.

stressor: diel-cycling hypoxia plus warming (factorial)
dose_treatment: 0.5 mg/L dissolved oxygen trough vs 100% saturation control; elevated vs ambient temperature (temperature set points not stated in abstract)
duration: 18 d per phase containing 13-14 d of diel cycling (from companion paper)
challenge: re-exposure to the same diel-cycling hypoxia and warming treatments 8 weeks later
readouts: tissue:shell growth ratio; tissue growth; shell growth
effect_magnitude: strong interactive effect of early-life hypoxia x warming on tissue:shell growth that manifested ONLY on re-exposure two months later; numeric effect sizes not given in abstract
replication: multi-phase laboratory experiment; 150 oysters per perforated container, 12 tanks (6 per DO treatment)
notes: Carryover effects were context-dependent: invisible in benign conditions and only expressed when the stressor returned. Energy reallocation between tissue and shell is the flagged fitness concern.

stressor: 18-compound pesticide and metal mixture
dose_treatment: nominal sum concentration 2.85 ug/L (measured sum 3.74 +/- 0.013 ug/L) vs clean filtered seawater
duration: 48 h (0-48 h post fertilisation)
challenge: none (baseline only); later-life traits and field deployment of 1-year-old spat
readouts: embryo-larval abnormality at 24 hpf; larval swimming behaviour; length and weight; epinephrine-induced metamorphosis rate; field survival
effect_magnitude: no significant difference in 24 hpf abnormality; swimming behaviour disturbed; exposed individuals longer and heavier at specific timepoints; LOWER epinephrine-induced metamorphosis rate; HIGHER field survival rate
concordance: Partial (significant global demethylation trend in exposed larvae alongside differential expression of Hox orthologues and cell-cycle regulators in gastrula embryos; no direct methylation-expression coupling shown)
notes: A 48 h embryonic window produced multi-scale latent effects detectable up to field deployment ~1 year later. Direction is genuinely mixed: impaired metamorphosis but improved field survival. Companion reproductive-endpoint paper (10.1016/j.scitotenv.2024.173569) reports F0 glycogen increase and higher 48 hpf reproductive success, plus F1 feminisation and accelerated gametogenesis.

stressor: 18-compound pesticide mixture
dose_treatment: nominal sum concentration 2.85 ug/L vs clean seawater
duration: 48 h (0-48 h post fertilisation) in each of two generations
challenge: direct F1 embryo-larval re-exposure to the same mixture in a 2x2 crossed design (F0 exposed/control x F1 exposed/control)
readouts: epinephrine-induced metamorphosis rate; field survival rate; growth
effect_magnitude: individuals descending from exposed parents had LOWER epinephrine-induced metamorphosis and LOWER field survival; the multigenerational (parental) effect had a greater influence on phenotype than direct exposure itself; negative interaction pattern for field survival (higher mortality when early exposure was combined with exposed parents)
concordance: Partial (RNA-seq and Methyl-seq in gastrula embryos and metamorphosis-competent pediveliger larvae showed clear F0-treatment-dependent discrimination; F1:F0 treatment interaction patterns for shell-secretion and immunity genes e.g. Calm and Myd88)
notes: MALADAPTIVE: parental conditioning made offspring WORSE, and the ancestral effect exceeded the effect of the animals' own exposure. Strongest pollutant multigenerational dataset in this table.

stressor: marine-heatwave temperature applied during gametogenesis
dose_treatment: 18.3 C (marine heatwave) vs 13.1 C (non-marine-heatwave control)
duration: 4 months (October 2020 to January 2021), timed to coincide with the local gametogenesis window
challenge: acute thermal tolerance trial on hatched blastula embryos across 7 temperatures (17.5, 20.5, 24.7, 26.4, 28.0, 29.8, 31.1 C); offspring also reared at 18 or 13 C
readouts: embryo LT50; embryo and larval body size (2D area) at early gastrula and prism stages; egg size; egg protein and lipid content; adult survival and spawning success
effect_magnitude: embryos from marine-heatwave-acclimated females had significantly higher LT50 than progeny of 13 C females; larger early gastrula and prism body size; eggs had higher protein concentration (egg size and lipid unchanged); COUNTERVAILING COST: marine-heatwave-acclimated adults had LOWER spawning success
replication: 3 replicate 37 L tanks per temperature condition, 10 adult urchins per tank (N=60 total)
notes: Adult-level trade-off: better offspring thermal tolerance but reduced adult spawning success. Offspring challenged immediately at spawning, so persistence window is zero; no test of how long the acquired tolerance lasts. No molecular data collected.

stressor: natural in-kelp vs outside-kelp variability in temperature, pH and dissolved oxygen during gametogenesis
dose_treatment: inside kelp forest (slightly elevated pH and temperature, more predictable low-frequency variability) vs outside kelp forest, Santa Barbara Channel
duration: 6 months of in situ conditioning spanning the gametogenesis period
challenge: larvae reared at 1053 vs 435 uatm pCO2 at 15 C, then acute thermal stress (LT50)
readouts: larval LT50; larval physiological response to maternal and developmental environment
effect_magnitude: within each larval pCO2 treatment, progeny from OUTSIDE-kelp-conditioned mothers had a 0.4 C higher LT50; larvae raised at high pCO2 (1053 uatm) were more susceptible to acute thermal stress regardless of maternal origin
notes: Natural conditioning contrast (field-conditioned mothers, not lab-dosed). Note the counterintuitive direction: mothers from the LESS buffered, less predictable outside-kelp environment produced the MORE thermally tolerant larvae, i.e. exposure to the more benign in-kelp refuge did not prime offspring.

stressor: ocean acidification and/or ocean warming
dose_treatment: OA pH 7.77; OW +2 C (29 C); OAW +2 C and pH 7.77; vs ambient control
duration: ~6 months, from the early juvenile stage through gonadogenesis and germline differentiation to the mature adult
challenge: embryos and larvae of acclimated parents reared in all four treatments to the 2-day pluteus stage
readouts: larval tolerance of acidification and of 29 C; larval arm length; egg size
effect_magnitude: larvae from OA and OAW parents were resilient to acidification and larvae from OW and OAW parents more tolerant of 29 C; BUT parental acclimation reduced larval arm lengths by as much as 21.4% and eggs were up to 21.8% smaller in females raised at 29 C
notes: Textbook TGP trade-off: stress tolerance gained at the direct cost of offspring size and maternal provisioning. First transgenerational climate-change study on a marine macroinvertebrate in which the F0 was acclimated across its whole reproductive life.

stressor: ocean warming plus acidification (mid-century and end-century scenarios)
dose_treatment: two near-future scenarios (projected mid- and end-21st-century elevated temperature plus elevated pCO2) vs present-day ambient; exact set points not stated in abstract
duration: 18 months of F0 acclimatization before spawning; F1 then held 25 months in the same conditions
challenge: F1 reared 25 months under the same conditions; a natural selective pathogenic mortality event occurred at 10 months of F1 age
readouts: test size; righting response time; respiration rate; survival through the pathogen event; capacity to spawn
effect_magnitude: Ambient-Ambient group was 21% larger and 31% faster in righting than all other groups; respiration depressed by 59% and righting slowed by 28% when parents came from near-future conditions; after the pathogen event size and respiration differences disappeared but a 29% righting deficit remained; spawning capacity 50% (ambient parents) vs 21% (other groups)
notes: MALADAPTIVE: significant NEGATIVE parental carryover effects, not acclimation. Physiological differences were erased by a selective mortality sweep while behavioural deficits persisted, i.e. decay was trait-specific. Assessments at 9, 10 and ~25 months.

stressor: ocean warming plus acidification
dose_treatment: +2 C above ambient temperature and 940 ppm pCO2 vs present-day ambient
duration: more than 6 years total; F0 wild adults plus F1 and F2 larvae and adults continuously exposed
challenge: F2 survivorship and size tracked to 720 d post-settlement; F3 larvae reared under climate-change or control conditions
readouts: F2 survivorship (>50% in all treatments) and test size; adult spawning performance; F3 larval arm and body length; F3 settlement success
effect_magnitude: no size difference among treatment groups up to 720 d post-settlement; significant NEGATIVE relationship between number of generations exposed to future ocean conditions and spawning performance; larvae could only be raised from control or 0.5-generation-exposed adults; larvae from both parental groups only reached settlement when raised under control conditions; reduced arm length under climate-change conditions plus smaller arm and body lengths from climate-change parents
notes: MALADAPTIVE and CUMULATIVE: negative parental effects did not diminish across generations and for some traits INCREASED. Authors state explicitly that no evidence of transgenerational acclimation was detected. The most direct multi-generation refutation of assisted-conditioning optimism in an echinoderm. | PERSISTENCE SEMANTICS: this value is an exposure / tracking window under continuous or repeated conditioning, NOT days elapsed after conditioning ended. Do not rank it against clean-recovery-gap rows such as Drury_2022 or Lafont_2017.

stressor: reduced pH (elevated pCO2)
dose_treatment: pH 7.7 and pH 7.4 vs control pH 8.0
duration: 2 months of parental exposure during gametogenesis
challenge: sperm activated at pH 8.0, 7.7 or 7.4; larvae from each parental group reared at pH 8.0 or 7.7 for 20 days
readouts: sperm motility, velocity, ATP content, ATP consumption, respiration rate; larval mortality; larval somatic growth
effect_magnitude: POSITIVE carryover on sperm: velocity decreased more slowly and ATP content was higher in sperm developed under acidified conditions (longer sperm longevity); sperm motility and respiration unaffected. NEGATIVE carryover on larvae: reduced survival of larvae from pH 7.4 parents, with additive negative effects of parental plus larval low pH; larvae from low-pH parents showed NO increased capacity to cope with OA and all groups showed reduced somatic growth at low rearing pH
notes: Stage-dependent REVERSAL: the same parental conditioning benefited the gamete stage and harmed the larval stage. Direct counterexample to positive-TGP expectations in echinoids.

stressor: reduced pH (acidified seawater)
dose_treatment: acidified seawater vs control seawater (pH and pCO2 set points not reported in abstract)
duration: two-generation rearing experiment (exposure length not reported in abstract)
challenge: larvae exposed to acidified seawater of the same pH as the parental treatment
readouts: larval survival; larval body size; larval morphology
effect_magnitude: larvae derived from parents acclimated to acidified seawater tended to have higher survival and showed less reduction in body size when exposed to the same pH, indicating a positive carry-over effect; no quantitative statistics in the abstract
concordance: Partial (expression patterns of larvae from acclimated parents were substantially different from those of larvae from non-acclimated and control parents, but no quantitative overlap reported)
notes: Closed access; dose, exposure duration and replication were NOT extractable, which is a notable reporting gap for one of the few clearly POSITIVE echinoderm OA carryover results. Species is a commercial edible urchin in northern Japan.

stressor: reduced pH (elevated pCO2)
dose_treatment: pH 7.72 / 1013 +/- 12 uatm pCO2 vs pH 8.06 / 412 +/- 6 uatm pCO2
duration: 2 months of adult conditioning at treatment pCO2 (preceded by 2 months acclimation to aquarium seawater; 4 months total in Menai Straits water before spawning)
challenge: larvae spawned and reared at ~1000 uatm; separate acute heat shock of 25 C for 1 h applied to adults and to 2 and 4 dpf larvae
readouts: larval transcriptome at 2, 3 and 4 dpf; HSP70 and HSP90 transcript induction by qPCR; larval morphometrics and abnormality rate
effect_magnitude: larvae from low-pH-acclimated adults up-regulated antioxidants (glutathione-S-transferase family), CypP450 detoxification genes and small HSPs, i.e. maternal transcript pre-loading; larvae reared in low pH had 25-40% abnormalities and significantly smaller body length:width ratio (F=8.035, p=0.005); early larvae could not mount a full heat shock response (2 HSP transcripts up at 2 dpf, 5 at 4 dpf vs 8 in adults)
concordance: Partial (transcriptional frontloading of antioxidants is concordant with previously reported improved larval performance under low pH, but larval morphology remained impaired)
replication: 5 females and 2 males successfully spawned per treatment with gametes pooled; 3 replicate larval cultures per treatment
notes: Mechanistic case for maternal pre-loading of protective transcripts. Caveat stated by the authors: the 2-month conditioning did NOT cover the whole reproductive cycle. Larval morphological impairment persisted despite the molecular priming.

stressor: elevated temperature
dose_treatment: ~+3 C above ambient (21 C vs 18 C ambient/laboratory control)
duration: ~15 months of dam and sire exposure
challenge: offspring reared at elevated (21 C) or ambient (18 C) temperature
readouts: fertilization success; hatchability; larval survival; larval size traits; abnormality; metamorphosis
effect_magnitude: no transgenerational effect on fertilization or metamorphosis; NEGATIVE transgenerational effects on hatchability and on most larval size traits; S. intermedius probably cannot achieve transgenerational acclimation to long-term elevated temperature for survival when offspring are also at elevated temperature; dam and sire effects were highly trait- and stage-dependent
concordance: Discordant (companion transcriptome study on the same F0/F1 animals, Shi et al. 2020, 10.1038/s41598-020-64872-x, found 1891 DEGs from parental thermal history at ambient and 2203 at high developmental temperature, with 904 shared DEGs changing in the same direction and FEWER DEGs between developmental temperatures in embryos of warm parents - a molecular frontloading signature that maps onto WORSE performance)
replication: breeding design with multiple dams and sires (n per cross not stated in abstract); companion transcriptome used 3 biological replicates per group (12 mRNA libraries)
notes: MALADAPTIVE: explicit failure of transgenerational acclimation despite 15 months of parental conditioning. Valuable because it pairs a negative phenotype with a strong molecular response (see concordance field).

stressor: maternal temperature shift timed to early vs late oogenesis
dose_treatment: mothers reared at 24 C then shifted to 18 C or to 30 C
duration: thermal cue applied at either an early or a late stage of oogenesis (exact durations not stated in abstract)
challenge: adult offspring acclimated to 18 or 30 C, then upper and lower thermal tolerance limits measured (onset of spasms, lethal temperature)
readouts: offspring upper and lower thermal tolerance limits measured at the adult stage
effect_magnitude: EARLY-oogenesis cue: mothers produced offspring with greater cold AND heat tolerance whenever mother-offspring temperatures did NOT match (anticipatory maternal effect); LATE-oogenesis cue: more tolerant offspring when temperatures PERSISTED across generations; the maternal effect disappears as traits approach the upper sublethal and lethal limits
replication: reproductive pairs isolated in 20 ml glass bowls (n per treatment not stated in abstract)
notes: The single most important design lesson in this table: the DIRECTION of transgenerational plasticity reverses depending on the timing of the maternal cue within oogenesis. Also notable that the maternal effect persisted into the ADULT offspring stage, against the usual expectation that maternal effects fade early.

stressor: ocean warming, ocean acidification, and their combination
dose_treatment: OW +3 C; OA pH -0.5 units; OWA +3 C and pH -0.5; vs control conditions
duration: full parental generation exposure across the life cycle
challenge: F1 exposed to the same OW, OA or OWA conditions (trans-generational) vs F1 exposed with control parents (within-generational)
readouts: fecundity; egg volume; juvenile growth rate; citrate synthase and electron transport system activity
effect_magnitude: trans-generational OW exposure FULLY alleviated the within-generation reduction in fecundity and egg volume, accompanied by increased metabolic activity; within-generation OA reduced juvenile growth rates and egg volume, and trans-generational OA exposure alleviated the growth deficit but could NOT restore egg volume (mean egg volume still ~10% below control); OWA had no negative impacts either within- or trans-generationally
replication: n=12 replicate breeding pairs per treatment for fecundity
notes: Explicitly framed as a test of human-assisted trans-generational conditioning as a conservation/restoration and aquaculture tool. Authors' conclusion is the useful caution: trans-generational exposure does not always improve traits and may not be a universally useful tool.

stressor: elevated temperature, and elevated temperature combined with elevated salinity
dose_treatment: 30 C (+3 C above the 27 C control) and 39 ppt elevated salinity vs control temperature and salinity; salinity alone was not tested
duration: entire lifespan, both within-generation and trans-generation; transplants performed at either the egg-mass or the juvenile stage
challenge: F1 exposed to the same elevated-temperature or temperature+salinity conditions; reciprocal transplants at egg-mass vs juvenile stage
readouts: juvenile growth rate; maximum body size; longevity; lifespan fecundity; citrate synthase and electron transport system activity
effect_magnitude: trans-generation exposure restored 20% (elevated temperature) and 21% (temperature plus salinity) of lifespan fecundity; under temperature+salinity, worms transplanted at the egg-mass stage grew slower with lower energy-metabolism enzyme activity but reached a larger maximum body size and lived longer than those transplanted as juveniles; trans-generation elevated temperature created a trade-off in which slower-growing juveniles had greater lifespan fecundity
notes: One of very few marine-invertebrate designs that includes SALINITY conditioning. Only ~20% of the fecundity deficit was recovered, i.e. partial rescue at best. The TIMING of the transplant itself generated life-history trade-offs, so developmental window matters as much as dose.

stressor: reduced salinity
dose_treatment: 26 ppt (low) vs 35 ppt (normal) seawater
duration: 2 weeks of adult exposure before reproduction; parents could be switched back and forth between salinities
challenge: in vitro fertilization and larval rearing in matched vs mismatched salinity; larvae switched from natal to non-natal salinity immediately after fertilization or 2 or 4 days after fertilization, with survival scored 2 days after each switch
readouts: sperm head area and tail length; egg morphology; fertilization success; larval survival
effect_magnitude: both mothers and fathers adaptively adjusted gamete phenotype to maximise performance in the parental salinity regime; sperm from low-salinity fathers were much smaller while egg morphology did not change; STRONG performance trade-offs whenever gametes experienced a salinity that did not match the parents; larvae switched on the day of fertilization had the LOWEST survival and later switches progressively higher survival; the parental-environment effect persisted for the whole larval phase
replication: 4 tubs per salinity treatment; sperm from 3 males and eggs from 3 females pooled per assay
notes: Best available demonstration that conditioning MANUFACTURES phenotype-environment mismatch: conditioned larvae are effectively unable to disperse to non-natal salinities, so gamete plasticity becomes a source of reduced connectivity. Parents could reverse the gamete phenotype based on their most recent experience, i.e. the memory is short and rewritable.

stressor: copper
dose_treatment: maternal colonies 300 ug/L Cu vs filtered seawater control; larvae subsequently 50 ug/L Cu vs filtered seawater control
duration: 6 h maternal exposure after larval release, then colonies returned to their field site to brood the test larvae
challenge: larval copper exposure at 50 ug/L, then settlement and growth to maturity in the field with survival and growth tracked weekly for 6 weeks
readouts: larval size at emergence; post-metamorphic survival; adult colony growth in the field
effect_magnitude: in the population with NO historical copper exposure (Boat Ramp), maternal copper exposure had a strong NEGATIVE carryover effect on adult offspring growth and survival, worst when larvae were themselves also exposed; in the population WITH a copper history (Marina) there was little to no maternal or offspring treatment effect on adult growth and survival, and those parents produced larger larvae on average and increased larval size in response to copper; significant effect of population on F1 growth after 6 weeks in the field (LMM p<0.05)
replication: split-brood design across 2 populations with copper and control maternal treatments crossed with copper and control larval treatments (n per cell not extracted)
notes: MALADAPTIVE in naive populations: the direction of transgenerational plasticity is itself a locally adapted trait. Persistence figure is the 6-week post-settlement field tracking window; the interval between the end of maternal exposure and larval release (field brooding) was not resolved to days.

stressor: copper
dose_treatment: copper exposure of maternal colonies vs toxicant-naive control (concentration not stated in abstract; cited by Neylan et al. 2022 as the basis for their 300 ug/L, 6 h protocol)
duration: laboratory copper exposure of maternal colonies followed by 1 week in the field to brood offspring
challenge: offspring copper resistance assay, then 6 weeks in the field under low vs high intraspecific competition
readouts: larval size; larval dispersal duration; larval copper resistance; post-metamorphic survival and performance
effect_magnitude: offspring of toxicant-exposed mothers were LARGER, more dispersive and more copper-resistant than offspring of naive mothers; BUT maternal exposure history had pervasive NEGATIVE effects on post-metamorphic performance, particularly survival, after 6 weeks in the field, especially under high intraspecific competition
notes: The canonical stage-reversal / maladaptive result: conditioning improves performance in one life-history stage and reduces it in the next. Author's interpretation is that this cost is precisely why pollution resistance is INDUCED rather than constitutively expressed. Persistence figure combines the ~1 week brooding period and the 6-week field assessment.

stressor: copper
dose_treatment: 100 ug/L Cu (as CuCl2.2H2O, Cu2+) vs artificial seawater control
duration: 6 h larval exposure
challenge: transplantation of settled juveniles to 2 field sites in 2 seasons (winter and summer), with survival and growth followed for months
readouts: larval attachment rate; metamorphosis success; post-metamorphic colony survival; colony growth
effect_magnitude: Cu accelerated larval attachment in both seasons but inhibited metamorphosis; colony survival fell to about two-thirds of control in summer and to about 20% of control in winter; the survival decline occurred abruptly 3-5 weeks after exposure in summer and 14 weeks after exposure in winter, by which time colonies were 10-15 mm diameter (~100 zooids) and had undergone several budding cycles; surviving colonies grew more slowly than controls
replication: 2 seasons x 2 sites in SE Australia; transplanted colonies followed individually (n not extracted)
notes: BEST persistence-window dataset in this table and a strong maladaptive case: a 6 h larval exposure produced NO detectable survival effect for 3-14 weeks and then caused catastrophic mortality, with season setting the latency. Authors note this is far later than any previously reported carryover effect and that the larva could not have accumulated enough Cu in 6 h to affect all zooids directly, implying an inherited/propagated cellular lesion. Persistence recorded as ~21 d (earliest summer detection of the survival drop, 3-5 wk); the winter latency was ~98 d (14 wk), so season roughly quadrupled the delay before the carryover effect appeared.

stressor: moderate hypoxia
dose_treatment: ~4 mg/L dissolved oxygen vs normoxic control
duration: from zygote to trochophore stage (duration in hours not reported in abstract)
challenge: hypoxia tolerance assessment at the grow-out (juvenile) stage
readouts: hypoxia tolerance; weight growth rate
effect_magnitude: juvenile abalone exposed to hypoxia during early development were MORE hypoxia-tolerant but showed SLOWER weight growth - an explicit growth-versus-survival trade-off; no quantitative statistics available in the abstract
concordance: Partial (carry-over phenotype attributed to strong selection on genes for signal transduction, autophagy, apoptosis and hormone regulation, plus long non-coding RNA regulation of DNA replication and repair, signal transduction, myocardial activity and hormone regulation)
notes: The only marine gastropod hypoxia-priming study located. Closed access, so exposure duration and persistence interval were not extractable. Important caveat: whole-genome resequencing showed strong SELECTION, so the authors cannot separate genetic selection from epigenetic carryover - this is differential survival as much as conditioning.

stressor: nickel and ocean acidification, singly and combined
dose_treatment: Ni 6 ug/L; pCO2 1000 uatm; and their combination; vs control seawater
duration: six consecutive generations (F1-F6) of continuous exposure, followed by one generation (F7) in clean seawater
challenge: one full generation of recovery in clean seawater (F7), with transcriptome compared against F6
readouts: development; reproduction; survival; nickel accumulation; transcriptome
effect_magnitude: Ni exposure compromised development, reproduction and survival across F1-F6, but ocean acidification ANTAGONISTICALLY alleviated Ni toxicity so that under combined exposure there was no disruption of Ca homeostasis and no inhibition of the calcium- or oxytocin-signalling pathways; the COST was a loss of transcriptome plasticity during recovery in F7, which limited the copepods' resilience when returned to their previous environment
concordance: Partial (F6 within-generation and F7 recovery transcriptomes compared directly; no quantitative overlap figure extracted)
notes: Rare and highly relevant design: explicitly tests RECOVERY after multigenerational conditioning. The finding that multigenerational acclimation carried a hidden cost - reduced capacity to revert - is exactly the kind of latent maladaptive outcome this lab should flag.

stressor: nanoplastics under ocean acidification
dose_treatment: nanoplastics combined with ocean acidification vs control (nanoplastic concentration and pCO2 set points not reported in abstract)
duration: ten consecutive generations of multigenerational exposure, plus transgenerational groups returned to clean conditions
generations: F0 through F10 exposed, plus unexposed F1T and F2T transgenerational groups
challenge: none (the F1T and F2T transgenerational groups were never themselves exposed to nanoplastics)
readouts: reproduction (fecundity); gene-specific DNA methylation
effect_magnitude: synergistic NEGATIVE effect of ocean acidification and nanoplastics on copepod reproduction across generations; reproductive impairment was still present in the F1T and F2T generations that had NEVER been exposed to nanoplastics
concordance: Concordant (the intergenerational reproductive impairments were associated with differential methylation patterns of specific genes)
notes: MALADAPTIVE across an exposure gap: harm inherited by descendants that never met the stressor, with a methylation correlate. Closed access, so doses and the recovery interval in days were not extractable.

stressor: elevated pCO2
dose_treatment: pCO2 900 uatm and 1550 uatm vs 400 uatm control
duration: two full generations at the treatment pCO2
challenge: reciprocal transplant of second-generation adults between pCO2 levels
readouts: fecundity (egg production rate); respiration/metabolic rate
effect_magnitude: second-generation adults showed a 29% decrease in fecundity at 900 uatm vs 400 uatm accompanied by a 10% increase in metabolic rate; reciprocal transplants showed that WITHOUT transgenerational effects fecundity would have fallen by as much as 67% at 1550 uatm; transgenerational effects held the loss at the 900-uatm level and removed the metabolic-stress signal, with respiration rates lower than at 900 uatm; the effect was fully reversible on transplant, i.e. phenotypic plasticity rather than fixation
concordance: Discordant (the molecular companion study on the same two-generation experiment, De Wit et al. 2015, 10.1111/eva.12335, found genes involved in RNA transcription strongly DOWN-regulated in high-pCO2 lineages EVEN AFTER transplant back to control pCO2, plus 1513 of ~747,000 SNPs with consistent replicate frequency shifts in RNA transcription, ribosomal function, ion transport and oxidative phosphorylation - so the fecundity phenotype reversed but the transcriptome did not)
replication: 6 laboratory populations (2 replicate populations per pCO2 level)
notes: One of very few studies to QUANTIFY how much of an apparent OA effect is masked by transgenerational plasticity (67% predicted loss vs ~29% realised). Critical caveat from the companion paper: over two generations, plasticity and selection cannot be separated (estimated mortality >50% per generation), and the molecular state did NOT return to baseline even though the phenotype did.

stressor: embryonic hypoxia (moderate and severe)
dose_treatment: moderate hypoxia 3.0-3.1 mg O2/L (HM) and severe hypoxia 2.0-2.1 mg O2/L (HL) vs normoxic control >6.5 mg O2/L (N); 23-24 C; ~30 psu
duration: zygote to planktonic trochophore stage (hours not stated); F0 then reared 2 years at ~6 mg O2/L to maturity
challenge: F1 offspring never exposed to hypoxia: 3-month common-garden growth and survival (4 to 7 months old, Mar-Jun 2024); acute hypoxia adhesion-duration (HYAD) assay at 1.13 +/- 0.23 mg O2/L and ~27 C for 27.2 h (June 2024)
readouts: F1 specific growth rate (shell length, shell width, weight); F1 survival in common garden; F1 hypoxia tolerance (HYAD50, proportion detached); microsatellite genetic diversity and differentiation; gill transcriptome of F0 and F1 adults
effect_magnitude: F0 treatment effect on F1 growth: SGR_SL, SGR_SW, SGR_W all p<2e-16 (two-way ANOVA), HL-N > HM-N = N-N; HYAD50 N-N 22.2 h vs HM-N and HL-N >27.2 h (Kaplan-Meier p=0.11, HR 1.45, NOT significant); detached after 27.2 h N-N 56.67% vs HM-N 45.95% vs HL-N 34.48% (chi-square p=0.0733, pairwise ns); common-garden survival N-N 87.78% vs HM-N 81.11% vs HL-N 90.00% (HM-N < HL-N, p=0.029)
concordance: Partial (23 DEGs shared across single-, inter- and multi-generational comparisons, 13 co-up incl. mthfr log2FC 1.32-2.10 and shmt1 1.24-1.87, 9 co-down incl. pif1, egr1; one-carbon pool by folate the only shared KEGG pathway; 158 DEGs specific to the inter-generational effect)
replication: F0 from 10 male x 30 female 'Fuhai #1' broodstock, one tank per F0 treatment; F1 parents 8F/5M (N), 9F/5M (HM), 10F/6M (HL); common garden 90 tagged juveniles per F1 group in 3 replicate tanks; HYAD 35 per group across 4 tanks; RNA-seq 3 replicates per group (27 libraries); microsatellites n=31 per group (n=7 HL-N)
notes: Covers the F1 OUTCOME of F0 embryonic hypoxia. Relationship to Shen_2022 (10.1021/acs.est.2c04975): this paper cites Shen 2022 and Dai, Shen, Ke et al. 2024 as the earlier within-generation (F0) work; its F0 zygotes were produced in Oct 2021 'as described by Dai, Shen, Ke et al. (2024)' at 3.0-3.1 and 2.0-2.1 mg/L, not the ~4 mg/L of the Shen_2022 row, and the paper does not say the F0 is the Shen_2022 cohort - same lab and strain, cohort identity not stated. Persistence ~970 d computed from the paper's month-level dates (F0 embryos Oct 2021, F1 HYAD June 2024). Major caveats: hypoxia-tolerance benefit is a non-significant trend; Fst 0.126-0.214 between N-lineage F1 and HM/HL-lineage F1 (vs 0.010-0.029 within lineage) - authors attribute this to selection during 2-year F0 culture and parent choice, so selection is confounded with non-genetic carryover; one tank per F0 treatment. 'More is less': re-exposing F1 embryos (HM-H, HL-H) partly cancelled the growth and tolerance benefit. HL-N suffered unexplained mass mortality in its original tank.

stressor: polyvinyl chloride microplastics (PVC-MP)
dose_treatment: nominal PVC-MP 3, 30 or 300 mg/L (P1-P3) vs bacterial-challenge control without MP (KP) and unexposed negative control (KN)
duration: 15 d PVC-MP pre-exposure
challenge: Vibrio parahaemolyticus immersion challenge (dose given as 10^x CFU/mL; exponent not legible in indexed abstract), survival recorded 7 d
readouts: survival; putative digestive-tract particle counts; hepatopancreas histopathology; FCR; SGR; net biomass gain; length gain
effect_magnitude: survival after challenge KN 83.33%, KP 66.67%, P1 48.33%, P2 26.67%, P3 21.67%; putative particle counts 17.66-18.14 particles/g in controls vs 74.28, 171.28 and 217.44 particles/g in P1-P3; dose-linked hepatopancreatic tubule dilation, degeneration, epithelial cytolysis and haemocytic infiltration; SGR, biomass gain and length gain declined, FCR increased
replication: 3 replicate containers per treatment (5 treatments); individuals per container not reported in abstract
notes: Closed to the tools available (Elsevier page and scite full text not retrievable), so dose units for Vibrio, shrimp size and whether MP exposure continued during the 7-d challenge are unknown. Life stage not stated in the abstract; 'Juvenile' assigned from the grow-out endpoints (SGR, FCR, length gain) - verify. The authors themselves flag that there is NO PVC-only treatment, so a priming (MP x pathogen) interaction cannot be separated from additive MP toxicity; particle identity not confirmed by FTIR/Raman; FCR not corrected for mortality. Species name as used by the authors (= Penaeus vannamei).; conditioning_stage set to not reported: the abstract does not state the life stage (screening guess was Juvenile)

stressor: lead (Pb)
dose_treatment: environmentally relevant Pb concentrations vs Pb-free control (values not reported in abstract)
duration: not reported
challenge: sequential exposure to salinities 5-25 and aerial temperatures 5-36 C
readouts: survival (Kaplan-Meier); tissue Pb concentration; gill or whole-tissue transcriptome (tissue not stated in abstract)
effect_magnitude: Pb raised baseline mortality, but elevated tissue Pb significantly attenuated temperature-driven mortality (partial cross-tolerance); reduced salinity increased heat vulnerability and weakened the protective effect of Pb; no numbers in the abstract
concordance: Partial (upregulation of cellular stress-response and detoxification genes, interpreted as transcriptional front-loading underpinning cross-tolerance; gene-expression responses modest overall)
notes: Gold OA (CC-BY) but the ScienceDirect page returned 403 and scite had no indexed text, so Pb doses, exposure duration, the gap before the salinity/heat challenge and mortality numbers could not be extracted - worth a manual PDF read. Arctic (Greenland-area) mussels; life stage not stated in abstract, 'Broodstock/adult' assigned for field mussels - verify. Pollutant-to-heat cross-tolerance, with a trade-off: higher baseline mortality from Pb itself.; conditioning_stage set to not reported: the abstract does not state the life stage (screening guess was Broodstock/adult)

stressor: combined ocean acidification and warming (AW) under three temporal scenarios
dose_treatment: AW vs ambient control (pCO2/pH and temperature set points not reported in abstract); Hg challenge 1 ug/L
duration: multigenerational F1-F4 under offspring-only AW, ancestral AW, or persistent AW scenarios (generation-specific timing not reported in abstract)
challenge: mercury 1 ug/L
readouts: development; reproduction; F4 transcriptome
effect_magnitude: offspring AW MITIGATED Hg toxicity; ancestral and persistent AW AGGRAVATED Hg toxicity, more so under persistent AW (compromised development and reproduction); no numbers in the abstract
concordance: Concordant (F4: offspring AW activated Hg efflux and energy production; ancestral and persistent AW suppressed antioxidant capacity, Hg detoxification and immune defence, most under persistent AW, matching the development and reproduction losses)
notes: Closed access. 'Decay = Persisted' rests on the ancestral-AW scenario (AW in earlier generations only) still aggravating Hg toxicity in descendants; exact timing of each scenario and whether development/reproduction were scored in every generation are not given in the abstract (multiple_timepoints set to No for that reason - verify). Valuable because it contrasts WHEN the climate stressor was experienced: recent (offspring) exposure was protective, ancestral exposure was maladaptive.

stressor: natural marine heatwave (MHW) exposure of adults
dose_treatment: adults sampled during natural MHW events vs adults sampled in periods without MHWs (in situ temperatures not reported in abstract)
duration: natural MHW events, 2021-2025 (event durations not reported in abstract)
challenge: copper embryotoxicity assay on offspring; offspring fertilization, larval development and morphology
readouts: fertilization rate; normal larval development; larval growth morphology (body width, total body length, postoral arm gap); larval Cu sensitivity
effect_magnitude: fertilization and early development unaffected by parental MHW; larvae from MHW-exposed parents had greater body width, total body length and postoral arm gap; Cu sensitivity did not increase; no numbers in the abstract
notes: natural conditioning contrast (adults collected during vs outside natural MHWs; not a manipulated exposure). Hybrid OA (CC-BY) but the ScienceDirect page returned 403 and scite had no indexed text, so MHW intensity, gap between MHW and spawning, and EC50 values were not extracted. Authors' a priori hypothesis was that MHW parents would yield MORE sensitive offspring; result was no added Cu sensitivity, which they read as tolerance/plasticity. Sampling across years confounds MHW status with year and gametogenic state.

stressor: sublethal heat shock
dose_treatment: 35 C for 1 h (ramped from 20 C) vs no heat shock (20 C)
duration: 1 h at 35 C, then 1 h recovery at 20 C
challenge: 96-h acute copper toxicity test (CuSO4, 0-500 mg/L Cu; LC50)
readouts: 96-h copper LC50 (adult male survival)
effect_magnitude: copper LC50 significantly increased in all 7 populations after heat shock (ratio test, p<0.05); per-population LC50 values in Fig. 5 / Table S4, not extracted; change in LC50 not related to latitude
concordance: Not evaluated (RNA-seq only on separate 24-h single-stressor exposures of two populations: 772 DEGs shared by heat and Cu in Bodega Bay, 642 in La Jolla, with common oxidative-defence and catabolic responses; primed vs naive animals under challenge were not sequenced)
replication: 12 adult males per plate per Cu concentration, concentrations with partial mortality repeated at least twice; 7 wild-collected populations lab-acclimated >=4 weeks; RNA-seq 2 pooled replicates (24-36 males) per treatment x 2 populations
notes: Short-term cross-protection (hours), not a lasting carryover; included as a priming result. Unidirectional: the reverse order (Coleman_2026b) reduced tolerance. 1-h recovery = 0.04 d persistence. Males used because less tolerant than females. Populations span a latitudinal thermal cline; acute heat and Cu tolerance co-vary across populations (LT50 vs LC50 R2=0.57, p=0.031).

stressor: copper shock
dose_treatment: 60 mg/L Cu (CuSO4) for 1 h vs clean filtered seawater, 20 C
duration: 1 h at 60 mg/L Cu, then 1 h recovery in clean seawater at 20 C
challenge: acute heat tolerance test (ramp from 20 C at 0.1 C/min to 35-42 C, 1 h hold, 1 h recovery; LT50)
readouts: median lethal temperature (LT50) of adult males
effect_magnitude: LT50 significantly decreased in all 7 populations after Cu pre-exposure (ratio test, p<0.05); per-population values in Fig. 4 / Table S4, not extracted
concordance: Not evaluated (see Coleman_2026a; transcriptomes were from single-stressor exposures only)
replication: 12 adult males per plate row per test temperature, temperatures with partial mortality repeated at least twice; 7 populations
notes: Cross-susceptibility, not protection. The priming dose was probably not sublethal: authors report that populations held 24 h in 60 mg/L Cu declined by 27% on average (Table S6), and suggest a lower Cu dose or longer recovery might reveal cross-protection. 1-h recovery = 0.04 d persistence.

stressor: decreased salinity (river-plume low salinity)
dose_treatment: 17-30 PSU vs control 34 PSU (carry-over effect reported for 30 PSU)
duration: range of larval exposure durations up to competent brachiolaria (durations not reported in abstract)
challenge: none (baseline only): competent brachiolaria induced to settle; metamorphosis and juvenile size at 5 d post-settlement
readouts: larval survival; normal development and morphology; juvenile production (metamorphic success); time to juvenile; juvenile size 5 d post-settlement
effect_magnitude: juvenile production highest in 30 PSU and 34 PSU control; faster transition to juvenile after extended 30 PSU exposure; but juveniles from 30 PSU larvae were SMALLER at 5 d post-settlement (negative carry-over on juvenile quality); lower salinity and longer exposure reduced larval survival and morphology; no numbers in the abstract
notes: Hybrid OA (CC-BY) but the Springer page redirects to a login handshake and scite had no indexed text, so exposure durations, settlement timing and juvenile-size statistics were not extracted - worth a manual PDF read. Not indexed in PubMed. Abstract gives Acanthaster spp. Hidden-cost pattern: mild low salinity looks benign or even accelerating at metamorphosis but yields smaller juveniles. Persistence not reported because the gap between end of exposure and settlement induction is not given; juveniles were scored 5 d after settlement. Framed around the terrestrial-runoff hypothesis for COTS outbreaks, with eReefs plume models.

stressor: gradual warming and constant high temperature over multiple generations
dose_treatment: increasing temperature 22 C to 26.9 C (+0.1 C three times a week) and constant 25 C vs control 22 C; 7 PSU; a 27 C treatment was dropped after one generation (only two females produced living nauplii)
duration: continuous exposure F0-F3 (increasing treatment ran 108 d), then half of each warmed line returned to 22 C for the F4 generation
challenge: none (return to control 22 C in F4 to test recovery, compared with lines kept warm)
readouts: hatching success (nauplii per female); prosome length; global DNA methylation; fatty acid content and composition (DHA, palmitoleic acid)
effect_magnitude: under continued warming, clutch size lower than control from F2 on (p<0.001) and negatively correlated with temperature (r=-0.22, p<0.001); in F4 the increasing-temperature-transposed group had higher hatching success than ALL other groups incl. control (p<0.001; p=0.012 vs high-transposed), and high-transposed exceeded both warm lines (p<0.001, p=0.031); global methylation in increasing-transposed significantly lower than its non-transposed line (p<0.001) and closer to control; prosome length in transposed groups stayed above control (p<0.001); DHA higher in increasing-transposed than increasing (p=0.036)
concordance: Partial (global methylation and hatching success both reverted toward or past control after return to 22 C; prosome length did not revert; global methylation only, no locus-level data)
replication: 5 replicate jars per treatment, each started with 80 ovigerous females per generation; F4 lines split into 5 kept-warm + 5 transposed replicates; 8 ovigerous females per replicate for reproduction; ~100 and ~80 adults per replicate for fatty acids and DNA; ONE incubator per temperature (no incubator replication)
notes: Key decay result: thermal effects on reproduction and global methylation were largely reversible within one generation back at control, and gradually warmed lines that were returned to control out-reproduced never-warmed controls. Acute 5 C rise caused reproductive collapse despite adult survival. Persistence not reported because generation length in days is not given (only 108 d for the increasing treatment overall); the recovery test spans one generation (F4). Caveats: closed lab stock since 1975 (low genetic diversity); temperature confounded with incubator; F3 reproduction and F0 high-temperature prosome data missing; females at F0 already carried egg sacs, so F3 is the first fully exposed generation.

stressor: repeated sublethal hypoxia (hypoxic preconditioning, HP)
dose_treatment: repeated sublethal low-oxygen exposure vs non-preconditioned control (HP DO level, bout length and number not reported in abstract)
duration: not reported
challenge: sustained hypoxia 1.5 +/- 0.1 mg/L DO for 15 d
readouts: hypoxia tolerance; gill apoptosis- and immunity-related gene expression; intestinal microbiota diversity and composition
effect_magnitude: after extended hypoxia, gill MyD88 EG 2.26 +/- 0.65 vs CG 0.96 +/- 0.29 (~2.3-fold), NF-kB 1.50 +/- 0.20 vs 0.81 +/- 0.31 (~1.8-fold), IkK 1.55 +/- 0.38 vs 0.65 +/- 0.12 (reported as ~4.0-fold), JNK 0.49 +/- 0.25 vs 1.44 +/- 0.51 (~0.34-fold), all p<0.05; higher gut alpha diversity (Ace, Chao, Sobs) and enrichment of Planctomycetota, Nitrospirota, Fusobacteriota; no survival numbers in the abstract
concordance: Concordant (authors link pre-activated but controlled apoptotic/immune signalling and higher gut diversity to HP-enhanced tolerance; association only)
notes: Gold OA (CC-BY) but MDPI returned 403 and scite had no indexed text, so the HP protocol, gap before challenge and any survival data were not extracted - worth a manual read. 'Improved' rests on the title and authors' conclusion; the abstract reports only molecular and microbiome readouts. Arithmetic flag: 1.55/0.65 is ~2.4-fold, not the ~4.0-fold stated in the abstract. Life stage not stated in abstract; 'Broodstock/adult' assigned - verify.; conditioning_stage set to not reported: the abstract does not state the life stage (screening guess was Broodstock/adult); gut microbiome (16S) also profiled, no schema code for it
